claims.text: The starting material is a Mg-transition-metal powder mixture with density below 6 g/cm³.
The starting powder mixture contains metastable eutectic phases.
A transient liquid phase will form in the proposed Mg-transition-metal system at 850 °C.
A temperature of 850 °C is below the volatility threshold of Mg and the transition metals in the proposed system.
Capillary forces from the transient liquid phase will rapidly densify the powder compact.
The transient liquid phase will accelerate atomic diffusion sufficiently to bypass solid-state kinetic barriers.
A subsequent 900 °C hold will dissolve residual eutectic or Heusler-type phases.
The two-stage treatment will stabilize a single-phase-like BCC or HCP matrix.
Oxygen and carbon impurities can stabilize an α-HCP phase and increase the α-to-β transition temperature.
An optimized cooling rate will prevent rapid dislocation-density reduction and high-temperature stability loss.
At 900 K and 1200 K, rapid lattice disorder and decreasing dislocation density can reduce hardness and elastic modulus.
Lower sintering temperatures can produce significant porosity because atomic diffusion is suppressed.
A standard homogenization treatment left eutectic grain-boundary formations and an undissolved Heusler-type phase in an Hf-containing alloy.
High-temperature exposure can produce oxide-layer gaps through volume expansion and diffusion.
The proposed two-stage treatment will produce a final relative density above 95%.
The proposed treatment will yield significantly less porosity than standard sintering at 950 °C.
The resulting single-phase-like material will have improved oxidation resistance because complex oxides and interfacial gaps are absent.
Sintering at 950 °C produced a measured density of 6.57 g/cm³, substantially below theoretical density.
Density fails below 800 °C because diffusion is suppressed.
Temperatures above 1000 °C cause excessive elemental volatility in the proposed Mg-transition-metal system.

contradictions.description: The protocol describes movement from 850 °C to 900 °C as a controlled cooling ramp, although this is a 50 °C temperature increase and therefore requires heating.
The conditions state that the sintering window is strictly constrained to 800–1000 °C, while experimental protocol C specifies sintering at 1050 °C.
The mechanism calls 850 °C a lower temperature that avoids behavior observed at 900 K, but 850 °C equals approximately 1123 K and is therefore substantially hotter than 900 K.
